main.title: Soul Edge
main.summary: Namco first showed Soul Edge in November 1995 before releasing the complete arcade fighting game in February 1996.

cards.text: Namco first showed Soul Edge in November 1995 before releasing the complete arcade fighting game in February 1996. It is the first installment in the Soulcalibur series. Introduced at the JAMMA trade show in November 1995, the full arcade game was released on February 20, 1996 (Soul Edge) and May 16, 1996 (Soul Edge Ver. II) on System 11 hardware, the same board used by Tekken and Tekken 2. Later in December, an upgraded and expanded version of the game was ported to the PlayStation; this version was renamed Soul Blade outside Japan and released in 1997.

Soul Edge is a 3D fighting game and was the second such game to be based on weapons, following Battle Arena Toshinden (itself preceded by the 2D Samurai Shodown series). The plot centers upon the eponymous sword, rumored to offer unlimited power to anyone who can find and wield it, leading to nine warriors attempting to pursue the tenth who is rumored to have the sword. The game was a commercial and critical success, with praise given to graphics, gameplay and characters. It was followed up with Soulcalibur in July 1998.

main.title: Pokémon Red and Green
main.subtitle: A collection designed to leave the screen
main.summary: A link cable turned different copies of a portable game into a reason to meet.

cards.heading: A collection made for trading
cards.text: Game Freak's Pokémon Red and Green launched in Japan in 1996. Capturing and developing creatures created a personal collection, while differences between versions encouraged players to trade through Game Boy's link cable.

cards.heading: The people behind the creatures
cards.text: Satoshi Tajiri's concept grew through a team whose work included Ken Sugimori's designs and Junichi Masuda's music and programming. Trading between players helped give the collection its meaning.

cards.heading: Two cartridges, one conversation
cards.text: Pokémon Red and Green began the series on Game Boy in Japan in 1996. A player travels through a world of towns, routes and battles while catching and raising Pokémon. Choosing a version begins the journey, but it also leaves reasons to talk to someone who owns the other one.

cards.heading: A cable makes a meeting
cards.text: Trading lets two players exchange Pokémon through a Game Link cable. Battles let them bring their trained teams into direct competition. The handheld's portability matters here: a collection can travel with its owner, then become something to compare and exchange face to face.

cards.heading: A collection that needs another person
cards.text: Differences between the versions and Pokémon that evolve through trading make exchange part of completing a collection. A design built around collecting creates a practical use for another player's cartridge, time and willingness to trade.

cards.heading: Red and Blue reach international players
cards.text: Pokémon Red Version and Pokémon Blue Version are popular 1996 role-playing video games (RPGs) developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy. They are the first installments of the Pokémon video game series and were first released in Japan as Pocket Monsters Red and Pocket Monsters Green, followed by the special edition Pocket Monsters Blue later that year. The games were released internationally in 1998 and 1999 as Pokémon Red and Pokémon Blue, while an enhanced version, Pokémon Yellow Version: Special Pikachu Edition, was released in Japan in 1998 and in other regions in 1999 and 2000.

cards.heading: Gym badges and the Pokedex
cards.text: The player controls the protagonist from an overhead perspective and navigates the fictional region of Kanto in a quest to master Pokémon battling. The goal is to become the Pokémon League Champion by defeating the eight Gym Leaders and the best Pokémon Trainers in the Kanto Region, the Elite Four. Another objective is to complete the Pokédex, an in-game encyclopedia, by obtaining all 151 Pokémon. Red and Blue use the Game Link Cable, which connects two Game Boy systems and allows Pokémon to be traded or battled between games. Both versions feature the same plot, and while they can be played separately, players must trade between both games to obtain all of the original 151 Pokémon.

cards.heading: Reception, remakes and rereleases
cards.text: Red and Blue were well-received, with critics praising the multiplayer options, especially the concept of trading. They received an aggregated score of 89% on GameRankings and are considered among the greatest games ever made, perennially ranked on top game lists including at least four years on IGN's "Top 100 Games of All Time". The games began a multibillion-dollar franchise whose games have collectively sold over 400 million copies worldwide. The Red and Blue versions were remade for Game Boy Advance (and later the Nintendo Switch for the 30th anniversary) as FireRed and LeafGreen (2004) while Yellow was remade for Nintendo Switch as Let's Go, Pikachu! and Let's Go, Eevee! (2018). The originals were rereleased on the Virtual Console service for the Nintendo 3DS in 2016 to commemorate their twentieth anniversaries.

cards.heading: A team becomes a memory
cards.text: A team records more than tactical preferences. The creature caught on an early route can remain beside us through later cities, carrying the memory of where the journey began. Levels and nicknames make continuity visible, allowing a collection of species to become a personal account of travelling together.

cards.heading: The first partner in Pallet Town
cards.text: The player begins in their hometown of Pallet Town in the Kanto Region (inspired by Japan’s Kantō region). After venturing alone into the tall grass, the player is stopped by Professor Samuel Oak, a famous Pokémon Researcher. Professor Oak explains to the player that wild Pokémon may be living there and encountering them alone can be very dangerous. He takes the player to his laboratory where the player meets Oak's grandson, a rival aspiring Pokémon Trainer. The player and the rival are both instructed to select a starter Pokémon for their travels out of Bulbasaur, Squirtle and Charmander. Oak's grandson will always choose the Pokémon which is stronger against the player's starting Pokémon. He will then challenge the player to a Pokémon battle with their newly obtained Pokémon and will continue to battle the player at certain points.

cards.heading: Atsuko Nishida and the design of Pikachu
cards.text: Pikachu's design emerged while Ken Sugimori was seeking more appealing, cute creatures for the collection. Atsuko Nishida joined the work with guidelines for an Electric-type Pokémon and its evolution. She created its early sprites within the Super Game Boy's colour limitations, before Sugimori unified the species through promotional drawings. Pikachu's planned line also changed: Raichu remained, while a further evolution called Gorochu was removed because of cartridge space. Pichu was introduced later, extending the family in the other direction.

cards.heading: Designing for beginners
cards.text: Masuda approaches each of his games with the mindset that a beginner should be able to easily play it. In view of this, his games begin in an easily approachable and accessible style, with more layers of complexity being introduced as the player progresses through the game. He believes that handheld systems provide an opportunity for social interaction that cannot be found on non-handheld console systems. He has stated that the continued use of 2D computer graphics has been integral to Pokémon's success.

main.title: Mickey’s Wild Adventure
main.subtitle: A journey through Mickey’s animated past
main.summary: Released for PlayStation in Europe on 1 March 1996, Mickey’s Wild Adventure brings the cartoon-inspired platforming of Mickey Mania to Sony’s console, with visual changes, new sequences and a CD soundtrack.

cards.heading: Mickey’s cartoon history reaches PlayStation
cards.text: Mickey’s Wild Adventure is the PlayStation edition of Mickey Mania, the platform game originally developed by Traveller’s Tales in 1994. Psygnosis developed this enhanced edition, published by Sony Computer Entertainment in Europe on 1 March 1996. Mickey travels through settings based on his animated films, from Steamboat Willie in 1928 to The Prince and the Pauper in 1990.

cards.heading: Jumping and marbles through changing scenery
cards.text: Players guide Mickey across platforms, avoid hazards and confront enemies by jumping on them or throwing marbles collected along the way. The stages change with the cartoons: the docks and machinery of Steamboat Willie give way to the castle and laboratory of The Mad Doctor. Platforming is interspersed with chases and obstacles that change how the player moves through each setting.

cards.heading: A distinct PlayStation edition
cards.text: The PlayStation edition enhances the graphics and adds a chase involving Willie the Giant. It also includes features shared with the Sega CD version, such as additional dialogue and a revised final confrontation in which pencils summon other versions of Mickey to help against Pete. The CD soundtrack features music by Andy Blythe and Marten Joustra, with additional music by Michael Giacchino.

main.title: Super Mario RPG
main.subtitle: When Mario Learns the Language of Role-Playing
main.summary: Super Mario RPG brought Nintendo's characters into a role-playing adventure developed with Square.

cards.heading: Mario enters a party
cards.text: Super Mario RPG brought Nintendo's characters into a role-playing adventure developed with Square. Released for Super Famicom in Japan in 1996, it sends Mario beyond the familiar rescue pattern after a new enemy takes over Bowser's castle. Towns, conversations and a travelling party give the journey a different scale.

cards.heading: A turn still needs a touch
cards.text: Battles use commands, but a button pressed at the right moment can strengthen an attack or improve defence. This keeps a small physical action inside the turn-based structure. Choosing a move and carrying it out are connected, leaving room for both planning and practice.

cards.heading: Unusual travelling companions
cards.text: Mallow and Geno join familiar figures including Bowser and Peach. Having a former enemy and the usual rescue target take roles in the party changes how Mario's world is encountered. The expanded cast gives battles different abilities while giving the adventure people to talk to, disagree with and rely on.

cards.heading: Nintendo and Square design an action-focused RPG
cards.text: Nintendo and Square began discussing the project in 1994, combining Miyamoto's wish for a Mario role-playing game with Square's interest in reaching audiences outside Japan. The team wanted Mario's actions to remain recognisable rather than simply replacing an RPG's cast. Jumping and dashing therefore became important to exploration, while discussions with Miyamoto removed unsuitable weapons but retained the hammer. An isometric view helped give the world depth. By 1995, programming, events and graphics were being brought together around that meeting of movement and role-playing systems.

main.title: Kirby Super Star
main.subtitle: A collection with a shared heart
main.summary: Kirby Super Star first appeared in Japan on March 21, 1996, as Kirby of the Stars: Super Deluxe. HAL Laboratory’s Super Famicom game gathered several adventures and smaller contests around Kirby’s ability to borrow an enemy’s powers. Europe later knew the same game as Kirby’s Fun Pak. Rather than stretching a single journey, director Masahiro Sakurai gave its individual stories distinct goals and their own conclusions.

cards.heading: A collection with a shared heart
cards.text: Kirby Super Star first appeared in Japan on March 21, 1996, as Kirby of the Stars: Super Deluxe. HAL Laboratory’s Super Famicom game gathered several adventures and smaller contests around Kirby’s ability to borrow an enemy’s powers. Europe later knew the same game as Kirby’s Fun Pak. Rather than stretching a single journey, director Masahiro Sakurai gave its individual stories distinct goals and their own conclusions.

cards.heading: An enemy becomes a companion
cards.text: A copied power can also become a Helper, an allied character controlled by the computer or a second player. Kirby remains the centre of the camera’s attention, while the companion shares the action. Sakurai described cooperation, richer fighting moves and the collection format as the project’s three main ideas. The same ability can support several attacks, giving both players something useful to do instead of leaving one to follow an already cleared path.

cards.heading: Short adventures, different rules
cards.text: Spring Breeze offers a compact journey through Dream Land; Gourmet Race combines running with a contest for food. The Great Cave Offensive turns exploration into a treasure hunt, while Revenge of Meta Knight gives its action a different pace and setting. The selection screen makes these changes visible before play begins. Later rereleases brought the original game to new Nintendo systems; the expanded Nintendo DS adaptation, Kirby Super Star Ultra, followed in 2008.

main.title: Panzer Dragoon II Zwei
main.subtitle: A dragon that grows with the journey
main.summary: Lundi and Lagi pursue an ancient airship through a rail shooter with branching routes and an evolving dragon.

cards.heading: Lundi and Lagi
cards.text: Panzer Dragoon II Zwei is Team Andromeda’s Saturn rail shooter, first released in Japan on 22 March 1996. Set before the original game, it follows Lundi and Lagi, an unusual creature he shelters against his village’s customs. When an ancient airship destroys the village, the two pursue it. Lagi begins the journey close to the ground before taking to the air. The player again aims the rider’s gun and the dragon’s lasers, while the flight passes through landscapes shaped by the machinery of a vanished civilisation.

cards.heading: Choosing a path in flight
cards.text: Some stages divide into alternative routes. Steering towards one branch changes the scenery and enemies encountered for the rest of that section, so a replay can follow a different journey through familiar territory. Threats still approach from several directions, with the radar helping the player decide when to turn the view. Shooting enemies also fills a Berserk meter. Activating it releases a sustained stream of homing lasers, providing a powerful answer when several attackers fill the screen and ordinary targeting leaves too much to handle at once.

cards.heading: A stronger companion
cards.text: Performance affects the travelling companion itself. Stage results take account of shooting, damage and other measures, and Lagi evolves into stronger forms as the adventure progresses. The player can therefore see the results of earlier flights in the dragon carrying Lundi. Finishing the game also opens Pandora’s Box, an extras menu for revisiting stages and changing settings. Yayoi Wachi’s score accompanies a story told through animated scenes and the series’ invented language, giving the short shooting campaign another reason to be followed through to its conclusion.

main.title: Resident Evil
main.summary: Resident Evil is a 1996 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Trapped in the Arklay mansion
cards.text: Resident Evil is a 1996 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation. It is the first main installment in Capcom's Resident Evil series. Set in the fictional Arklay mountain region in the Midwest, players control Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine, members of the elite task force S.T.A.R.S., who must escape a mansion infested with zombies and other monsters.

cards.heading: Several designs become survival horror
cards.text: Resident Evil was conceived by the producer Tokuro Fujiwara, inspired by the limitations on his 1989 horror game Sweet Home. It was directed by Shinji Mikami. It went through several redesigns, first as a Super NES game in 1993, then a fully 3D first-person PlayStation game in 1994 and finally a third-person game. Gameplay consists of action, exploration, puzzle solving and inventory management. Resident Evil established many conventions seen later in the series, and in other survival horror games, including the inventory system, save system, and use of a vitals-monitoring system instead of a health counter.

cards.heading: Atmosphere reaches a large audience
cards.text: Resident Evil was praised for its graphics, gameplay, sound, and atmosphere, although it received criticism for its weak dialogue and voice acting. It was an international best-seller, and became the highest-selling PlayStation game at the time. By December 1997, it had sold about 4 million copies worldwide and had grossed more than US$200 million.

cards.heading: A mansion becomes a wider franchise
cards.text: Resident Evil is often ranked as one of the greatest and most influential video games ever made. It is credited with defining the survival horror genre and with returning zombies to popular culture, leading to a renewed interest in zombie films by the 2000s. It created a franchise including video games, films, comics, novels, and other merchandise. It has been ported to Sega Saturn, Windows and Nintendo DS. Its sequel, Resident Evil 2 was released in 1998. Both the game's remake and prequel were released on GameCube in 2002.

features.title: Who controls the blind spot
features.summary: Resident Evil's teams rebuilt the conditions of fear.

cards.heading: Fear arrives before the attack
cards.text: In a 1999 interview, Shinji Mikami described fear building before an attack, when the player suspects something beyond the frame. He recalled experimenting with a first-person version of Resident Evil before choosing fixed viewpoints. Framing and cuts let the team arrange blind spots, controlling how much of a room the player could see at once.

cards.heading: The player needs room to answer
cards.text: Mikami recalled that Capcom's interest in Sweet Home's systems helped start the project. He wanted players to have opportunities to react differently from the doomed characters he had watched in horror films. The resulting design questioned whether every enemy should be killed and whether the player should always be stronger. Strategy mattered alongside the immediate ability to fight.

cards.heading: A sequel struggles to agree
cards.text: Producer Hiroyuki Kobayashi recalled that Resident Evil 4 went through successive versions while the staff struggled to agree on what the game should become. He credited Mikami's arrival as director with bringing the eventual direction together. The overhaul required the producer and development team to manage disagreements and revise material before the finished game's approach was settled.

cards.heading: Another person changes the fight
cards.text: Protecting Ashley added another demand to Resident Evil 4's combat. Kobayashi described keeping her close, avoiding shots that could hit her and reacting when she noticed danger behind Leon. He credited the programmers who made these interactions work. During a crowded fight, players had to manage the companion's position alongside their own movement and aim.

main.title: Street Fighter Alpha 2
main.summary: Street Fighter Alpha 2, known as Street Fighter Zero 2 in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1996 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.heading: The Alpha sequel
cards.text: Street Fighter Alpha 2, known as Street Fighter Zero 2 in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1996 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. The game is the sequel to the previous year's Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams and features a number of improvements, such as new attacks, stages, endings, and gameplay features. It was ported to the PlayStation, Sega Saturn and Super Nintendo home consoles globally in 1996, and later a Windows port. It was followed by Street Fighter Alpha 3 in 1998.

cards.heading: Building a Custom Combo
cards.text: Street Fighter Alpha 2 retains most of the new features introduced in the original Street Fighter Alpha, such as the three-level Super Combo gauge, Alpha Counters, Air-Blocking, and Fall Breaking. The main new feature in the game is the inclusion of the Custom Combo system (Original Combo in Japan), which replaces the Chain Combos from the first Alpha. If the Super Combo gauge is on Lv. 1 or above, the player can initiate a Custom Combo pressing two punch buttons and a kick or one punch button and two kicks. The player can then perform any series of basic and special moves to create a Custom Combo until the Timer Gauge at the bottom of the screen runs out. The characters Guy and Gen can still perform Chain Combos, but only to a limited extent. Additionally, each character now has two Alpha Counters instead of just one: one that can be performed with a kick button and another with a punch button.

cards.heading: Rivals interrupt the campaign
cards.text: The single-player mode, much like the original Street Fighter Alpha, consists of eight matches against computer-controlled opponents, including a fixed final opponent whose identity depends on the player's selected character. Each character also has a secret "rival" whom they can face during the course of the single-player mode. After meeting certain requirements, the rival will interrupt one of the player's matches and exchange dialogue with the player's character, and the player character will then fight the rival instead. With Akuma now a regular character, a more powerful version of the character dubbed "Shin Akuma" replaces him as a secret opponent. Unlike Super Turbo and the original Alpha, Shin Akuma challenges the player before the player's final opponent, rather than as an alternate final boss.

cards.heading: Newcomers join the roster
cards.text: The game brings back all thirteen characters from Street Fighter Alpha, with M. Bison, Akuma, and Dan now being immediately selectable as playable characters. In addition to the Alpha roster, Alpha 2 includes Dhalsim and Zangief, both from Street Fighter II; Gen, an assassin from the original Street Fighter; Rolento, a member of the Mad Gear gang who originally appeared in Final Fight; and newcomer Sakura, a Japanese schoolgirl who takes up street fighting after witnessing one of Ryu's battles. The game also features a "classic-style" alternative version of Chun-Li where she is wearing her outfit from the Street Fighter II series.

cards.heading: Balancing ordinary and special attacks
cards.text: Capcom senior planner Shinji Mikami explained that the team balanced Alpha 2 around its own roster, including the newcomers. Damage from ordinary attacks was increased to help maintain that balance. The designers wanted normal hits to remain important alongside special moves, giving players reasons to consider the basic attacks available to each character.

cards.heading: Animated adaptations
cards.text: Both Manga Entertainment/A.P.P.P. and Group TAC developed OVA adaptations based on the game, titled Street Fighter Alpha: The Animation (2000) and Street Fighter Alpha: Generations (2005), which were both co-produced by Kaoru Mfaume. All of the characters except Gen and Dan also have roles in the Canadian-American cartoon Street Fighter: The Animated Series.

cards.heading: Regional roster differences
cards.text: Street Fighter Alpha 2 was released under the title Street Fighter Zero 2 in Japan, Asia, and South America. The North American and European versions of Alpha 2 feature three additional characters who were not in the Zero 2 version: Evil Ryu and alternative versions of Dhalsim and Zangief known as EX versions, where they use their movesets from the Street Fighter II series and do not have access to the Super Combo gauge. These three characters were selected by Capcom USA.

main.title: Dragon Force
main.subtitle: The armies of Legendra
main.summary: Dragon Force is J-Force and Sega's strategy role-playing game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 29 March 1996.

cards.heading: The armies of Legendra
cards.text: Dragon Force is J-Force and Sega's strategy role-playing game, first released for Saturn in Japan on 29 March 1996. The player leads one of Legendra's rulers, moving armies between castles while the continent faces a returning ancient threat. Each general can command up to a hundred soldiers, allowing two hundred figures to meet in a single battle. Those encounters give the campaign its striking spectacle, but the journey also depends on recruiting officers, supporting their growth and deciding where each force will be needed next.

cards.heading: A hundred soldiers under one general
cards.text: When opposing armies meet, the game moves from the map to a battlefield. The player chooses a general, troops and a formation after seeing the enemy's selection, creating an opportunity to answer that force with a suitable arrangement. Soldiers fight in real time, while menus allow orders and special attacks to interrupt the action. Defeating a general can capture or injure an opponent. If both sides lose their soldiers, the remaining commanders may end the encounter in a duel, making the officers important beyond the size of their armies.

cards.heading: Building the next campaign
cards.text: Between campaigns, administrative periods let the ruler reward generals, recruit new officers, persuade prisoners to join and strengthen castles. Rewards can increase an officer's troop capacity, so a useful commander becomes more valuable through service. Different rulers begin with their own circumstances and followers, giving another campaign a different route across the same continent. Working Designs translated the North American edition, later used for the European release. Dragon Force connects its crowded battles to these quieter decisions, allowing the army on screen to reflect relationships and preparations made on the map.

main.title: Digital Anvil
main.subtitle: Origin veterans establish a new studio
main.summary: On April 8, 1996 a group made up largely of Origin Systems veterans founded Digital Anvil in Austin.

cards.heading: A studio founded in Austin
cards.text: Origin Systems veterans founded Digital Anvil in Austin on April 8, 1996. Chris Roberts brought his experience with Wing Commander to a studio planning ambitious games with a cinematic presentation. Digital Anvil released Starlancer, Freelancer and Brute Force during a history that included investment, acquisition by Microsoft and eventual closure. Its projects required the team to balance expansive ideas with production schedules and resources.

cards.heading: Chris Roberts leaves Origin
cards.text: After Origin's growth around Wing Commander, Roberts and other veterans wanted to work within a more compact studio. Their plans still involved technologically ambitious games and a close relationship with cinematic storytelling. Building such projects required investment, tools and time, giving the new team a substantial production task alongside the freedom of an independent company.

cards.heading: Completing Freelancer
cards.text: Freelancer combined trade, combat, factions and travel between systems in an accessible space game. Development stretched beyond its original plans. Microsoft acquired Digital Anvil in 2000, the project was reduced in scope and Roberts left its leadership. Released in 2003, the finished game retained the trading and combat that had been central to the studio's vision while reflecting changes made during production.

cards.heading: Microsoft and the studio’s closure
cards.text: Microsoft acquired Digital Anvil in December 2000. Some projects were sold and others completed within the new structure, including Freelancer and Brute Force. Staff were redeployed in 2005, and the company was formally dissolved in January 2006. Its founders and employees continued their careers elsewhere after the studio's work on space games and Xbox production.
